text:
B: Hello, can you hear me all right?
A: Yes. Hello. I'm Joanne.
B: Nikhil. Nice to meet you. Where are you calling from?
A: Frome. In Somerset. You?
B: Thornton Heath, which is Croydon, basically. South London. Er, I have to say I noticed the bowls behind you in the photo, on the shelf. Are those yours?
A: They are. Erm. They're not very good. I do a class on a Tuesday.
B: The glaze colours were nice, that blue-green. I wouldn't know how to begin.
A: My tutor says my glazes are brave. I think that means she doesn't like them.
B: Brave. Maybe it means she does, a bit. What do you do in the day?
A: I'm a senior carer. Shift lead in a dementia home. Twelve-hour shifts mostly. So the pottery's sort of where I go to not think.
B: That makes sense. Twelve hours is a lot. What does a shift lead actually do?
A: Run the floor. Medication rounds, care plans, keep an eye on the carers. And the residents, obviously, that's the point of it. People think it's just washing and feeding. It isn't. You're watching all the time, someone's not eating, someone's walking differently. You notice before the doctor does, usually.
B: Mm. Noticing small things before they become big things. That's a bit like my job, actually, although mine's a lot less important.
A: What's yours?
B: I'm a CAD technician for an engineering consultancy. I draw the ductwork and pipes and electrics for buildings. And the main thing really is spotting where a duct is going to hit a steel beam before somebody on site discovers it the hard way. So, er, noticing. But with drawings, not people.
A: Right. I'd assumed you were an academic. From the photo. All the books.
B: No, no. Diploma in Pune, then a part-time HNC at a college in South London. The books are just, I like reading. Architecture mostly, some novels.
A: What sort of novels?
B: Translated, a lot. Portuguese at the moment, because I'm learning on an app. Saramago. I'm struggling with him a bit.
A: I went to Lisbon once. With a friend. I loved it.
B: Oh, really? We went, my wife and I, a few years ago. What did you love about it?
A: The tiles, mostly. On the outside of the houses. And the bookshops. There was one, very old, sort of narrow, I could have stayed in there all day. My friend wanted the bars, I wanted the bookshops.
B: Bertrand, maybe? The oldest one. Near the Chiado.
A: Possibly. I don't remember the name. I bought a Pessoa I still haven't read.
B: Ha, I probably have the same Pessoa, also not finished. The tiles, though, I took hundreds of photographs. Swati was very patient. Do you think the tiles feed into the pottery? Because it's the same kind of colours.
A: Erm. I've never thought about that. Maybe. I just pick the colour I like on the day.
B: Brave.
A: Yes, all right. Do you travel much, then?
B: A fair bit. Cities. Berlin, Porto, Istanbul. And Pune every year to see my parents. You?
A: Cornwall. Pembrokeshire. Somewhere with walks and a dog-friendly cottage. I'd like Iceland one day, but, you know, money. And the dog.
B: Iceland would be amazing. There's a concrete church in Reykjavik that I've wanted to—
